title: Perceived Negative Workplace Gossip, Mental Health, and Professional Life Among Employees in Greece: A Cross-Sectional Study
content: This study examined the association between perceived negative workplace gossip and the mental health and professional life of employees working outside the healthcare sector in Greece. A cross-sectional study was conducted with 432 employees of the public and private sectors between April and June 2026. Validated instruments were used to assess perceived negative workplace gossip, symptoms of anxiety and depression, quiet quitting, work engagement, organization-based self-esteem, job satisfaction, burnout, and turnover intention. Multivariable linear and logistic regression models were adjusted for sex, educational level, and work experience. Higher levels of perceived negative workplace gossip were associated with more symptoms of anxiety and depression, higher scores on the three dimensions of quiet quitting (detachment, lack of initiative, and lack of motivation), and more burnout. Perceived negative workplace gossip was also associated with lower work engagement, organization-based self-esteem, and job satisfaction, and with higher odds of high turnover intention. These findings suggest that perceived negative gossip is related to poorer mental health and less favorable work attitudes among employees outside healthcare. Organizations may consider clearer formal communication and better supervisory practices to limit negative gossip, while longitudinal studies are needed to establish the direction of these associations.
